Kit

kit/combat — health, abilities, effects, projectiles

7 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Replicated combat state and local projectilesHealth and abilitiesBlocks or low-level helpersStatus effectsProjectilesCast origin and leashFire announcementsPredicted hpPublishing combat statsPoolsWorked exampleTiming and validation constraints

Use kit/combat to apply damage, check ability costs and cooldowns, maintain timed effects, and simulate projectiles. Coop games can display a shot immediately on the shooter's screen while the host decides damage. The package also provides helpers for recording damage, kills, and deaths in the session stat registry; the game calls them at impact and death.

The network examples here use coop replication: Predicted_Hp displays local damage until an hp delta arrives, the host validates hits, and fire_announce distributes projectile visuals. A sim-lane game instead schedules commands within ticks and can judge hits with lag comp. Health may remain reliably replicated, as in Quickdraw; state that must replay with a tick uses predict fields. Fired shots can use predicted projectile entities or declared presentation events; see sim.md.

Range/cone checks and damage arithmetic are pure and replay-safe. The Cooldowns and ability bundles lack simulation-descriptor test coverage; do not put them on the simulation lane without adding that coverage.

Replicated combat state and local projectiles#

Declare combat state as ordinary replicated entity fields: hp: i32, cds: [4]u16, and fx: [4]Effect. kit/net sends their changes as deltas. The operations in kit/combat are deterministic, allocation-free, and independent of Godot, so a predicted command and an authority tick apply the same checks when given the same bytes.

In this coop pattern, projectiles are local simulations rather than replicated entities. The shooter predicts the cast's cost and cooldown immediately. Each peer draws its own visual with the same projectile math, while the host's simulation validates hits and applies damage.

Health and abilities#

Odin
// Apply damage using the game's hp integer type, clamping at zero.
// `dealt` reports applied damage (0 on a corpse) for hit credit;
// `died` reports the killing blow exactly once.
hurt :: proc "contextless" (hp: ^$T, dmg: T) -> (dealt: T, died: bool)
// Restore `amount`, clamped to `maximum`. Reviving a corpse is a heal from 0
// The caller decides whether healing from 0 is allowed.
heal :: proc "contextless" (hp: ^$T, maximum: T, amount: T)
// The i32 helper over `hurt` returns only `died`. It clamps hp at zero
// and reports each death once. hit and play.Health both call `hurt`,
// so raw fields and blocks apply the same damage and death rules.
hit :: proc "contextless" (hp: ^i32, amount: i32) -> (died: bool)

Ability_Def :: struct {
	name:     string, // for ability bars / logs; kit/combat never allocates it
	cooldown: u16, // net ticks
	cost:     i32, // spent from whatever resource the game passes in
}
// Check readiness and cost, then pay and start the cooldown. Prediction
// and authority call this from inside the ability's command proc.
ability_try :: proc "contextless" (cds: []u16, slot: int, def: Ability_Def, resource: ^i32) -> bool
ability_ready :: proc "contextless" (cds: []u16, slot: int) -> bool
// The authority's per-net-tick decay (clients receive it as deltas).
abilities_tick :: proc "contextless" (cds: []u16)

// Embed the `cds: [N]u16 gd:"replicate"` field with `using cd:
// kcombat.Cooldowns(3)`. The array replicates as a flat field;
// cd_try/cd_ready/cd_tick pass `cds[:]` to the underlying helpers.
Cooldowns :: struct($N: int) {
	cds: [N]u16 `gd:"replicate"`,
}

Define abilities as code constants. Cavecrawl's ROCK_ABILITY has cooldown = 20, which lasts one second at 20 Hz. A predicted cast is a command procedure; generated policy runs it for client prediction and authority execution. This example is from spelunker.odin:

Odin
@(gd_command = knet.ACTION_OWNER_PREDICTED)
spelunker_heal :: proc(self: ^Spelunker) -> bool {
	if self.hp <= 0 || self.hp >= MAX_HP {return false} // reject dead or already fully healed targets
	if !kcombat.ability_try(self.cds[:], 1, HEAL_ABILITY, &self.stamina) {return false}
	self.hp = min(self.hp + HEAL_AMOUNT, MAX_HP)
	return true
}

Check ability_ready before issuing the command, as input.odin does. A locally refused prediction is still sent, so repeated input while an ability is unavailable would send requests the host must reject. kit/ui's ability bar renders the same cds and definitions.

Blocks or low-level helpers#

Start with the play blocks for entity health and named abilities:

  • play.Health combines hp, maximum health, a damage-change notification, and the current health fraction.
  • play.Ability generates a cast command on the containing entity, replicates cooldown configuration, and handles command acceptance and rejection.

play.Health calls hurt for its clamp, and play.Ability calls cast_gate for its readiness check. Blocks and raw fields therefore use the same rules for readiness and death. Both use kcombat.Ability_Def. The game's definition table retains names and costs because a replicated blob cannot contain a string and a wire command cannot carry a resource pointer. That table also feeds kit/ui's ability bar for either blocks or slot arrays.

Use the low-level helpers for cases that need different storage or checks:

  • ability_try checks and spends a resource when casting. Check the same definition row before issuing and in the authority hook.
  • Cooldowns(N) stores slots indexed at runtime, such as castable inventory items that cannot be represented by named block fields.
  • hit/hurt operate on hp outside an entity block, such as a transient value or a separate pool.

Cavecrawl and Homestead use the low-level helpers; Scrapyard uses blocks. See kit/net — composing verbs from embedded blocks.

Status effects#

One buff/debuff is 4 POD bytes, embedded as a fixed array (fx: [4]Effect); kind 0 (EFFECT_NONE) is the empty slot.

Odin
Effect :: struct {
	kind:  u8,
	power: i8,
	left:  u16, // ticks remaining
}
// Refresh an effect of the same kind with the strongest power and longest
// duration, or use the first empty slot. Return false when all slots are busy.
effects_add :: proc "contextless" (fx: []Effect, kind: u8, power: i8, ticks: u16) -> bool
// The authority decrements durations each net tick and clears expired slots.
// A hand-written {kind, left = 0} row also clears immediately,
// preventing underflow into a 65535-tick duration.
effects_tick :: proc "contextless" (fx: []Effect)
effect_of :: proc "contextless" (fx: []Effect, kind: u8) -> (Effect, bool)

Projectiles#

The host uses the projectile math to judge damage, and peers use it to animate local kit/fx tracers. They start from the announced origin and velocity; network transit delays when remote peers begin their visuals.

Odin
Projectile :: struct {
	pos:  [3]f32,
	vel:  [3]f32, // velocity per tick, not per second
	left: u16, // ticks to live
}
Target :: struct {
	id:     u32,
	pos:    [3]f32,
	radius: f32,
}
// Advance one tick. False = time to remove it (this tick still happened —
// hit-test the swept segment before discarding).
projectile_step :: proc "contextless" (p: ^Projectile) -> (alive: bool)
// First target the tick's travel touches (earliest along the path wins, not
// nearest to the muzzle). `from` is the position before projectile_step.
projectile_hit :: proc "contextless" (from: [3]f32, vel: [3]f32, targets: []Target) -> (best: Target, ok: bool)

Cast origin and leash#

Include the shooter's local cast origin in the throw command. With owner-streamed movement, the host receives the shooter's position after a delay. Launching from that older copy makes the authority projectile follow a different path from the shooter's visual. The host bounds the supplied origin with leash:

Odin
// leash clamps a claimed point into a disc of radius r around anchor.
leash :: proc "contextless" (claimed, anchor: [3]f32, r: f32) -> [3]f32

Origins within the permitted latency offset pass unchanged; larger displacements are clamped to the allowed distance. Call it in the command procedure, as spelunker_throw in spelunker.odin does. During local prediction, claimed == anchor, so the same call leaves the origin unchanged.

Fire announcements#

When the host accepts a cast, it broadcasts a Fire through the session's app channel (session.md). Each peer simulates that projectile locally for presentation. The shooter starts at cast time (zero RTT); other peers start when the announcement arrives. The announcement and later hp delta travel the same one-way path, aligning remote visual impacts with health changes.

Odin
Fire :: struct {
	shooter:   knet.Player_Id, // actual causer; echo suppression uses `predicted`
	origin:    [3]f32,
	vel:       [3]f32, // per tick; a no-flight kind may use it for spatial data such as radius
	ttl:       u16,
	kind:      u8,  // game-defined (which ability/visual)
	arg:       u16, // the game's payload word beside kind — an ability/status id, a variant
	                // (use arg for ids; packing them into vel.z limits the payload to 2D)
	predicted: bool, // the shooter's screen drew this at cast time; skip its echo.
	                 // false = present on every screen, including the causer's
}
fire_write :: proc(w: ^knet.Writer, f: Fire)
fire_read :: proc(r: ^knet.Reader) -> (f: Fire, ok: bool)

Fire announcements default to FIRE_TAG :: 1; the other app tags are comms 0, xfer 2, and sim 3. Store a listener in a struct field so each session has its own route rather than sharing package globals:

Odin
fire_announce :: proc(s: ^ksess.Session, f: Fire, tag: u8 = FIRE_TAG)   // authority only; asserts on a client
fire_announce_to :: proc(s: ^ksess.Session, peer: ksess.Peer_Id, f: Fire, tag: u8 = FIRE_TAG) // addressed
fire_listen :: proc(fr: ^Fire_Route, s: ^ksess.Session, tag: u8 = FIRE_TAG)
fire_poll :: proc(fr: ^Fire_Route) -> (f: Fire, ok: bool)
fire_route_destroy :: proc(fr: ^Fire_Route)

Use fire_announce_to to send a recent transient event to one newly joined player. Take that player's Peer_Id from the roster on Ev_Player_Joined; rebroadcasting would make existing peers process the event again.

fire_poll drops a predicted fire when its shooter is the receiver, because that screen already presented it at cast time. This also drops an addressed replay to the original caster after reconnecting with the same identity. That is appropriate for transient one-shots, but makes fire announcements unsuitable for persistent effects. Represent a standing zone or lingering glow as an entity so new and returning players receive its current state in the world snapshot. Use fire_announce_to only for the remaining part of a transient effect a particular peer should see.

Only the authority may call fire_announce; it asserts on a client, and receivers discard announcements from non-host authors. The listener stores events in ksess.App_Queue, also used by comms, xfer, and albums. It does not invoke game callbacks. Drain the route with fire_poll each frame on the game's stack.

The authority loops its own announcement into its local route, so the same polling code presents events on the host and clients. A predicted fire skips the shooter's echo. A host-produced event with predicted = false, such as a nova or reaction, appears on every screen, including the actual causer's.

Odin
// host, when the command hook confirms a cast:
kcombat.fire_announce(&self.ses, f)

// ready(), every peer:
fires: kcombat.Fire_Route   // a field on your game struct
kcombat.fire_listen(&self.fires, &self.ses)

// Each frame, poll and draw on every peer, including the host.
// A predicted fire skips its shooter; call fire_route_destroy on exit.
for {
	f, ok := kcombat.fire_poll(&self.fires)
	if !ok {break}
	// draw the rock
}

Raw fire_write/fire_read stay public for games that need a different envelope.

For tick-based cooldowns and kit/ai's director, read ksess.session_tick_no(s) instead of maintaining a parallel counter that can drift across resume and host migration. A campaign clock is different: the game must persist it in its save blob because session ticks cover only the session's lifetime. Cavecrawl uses its saved host_ticks to schedule respawns across saves.

Predicted hp#

When your local rock visually contacts a body, the health you display may dip immediately. The dip lives in a presentation overlay and cannot change authoritative health:

Odin
Predicted_Hp :: struct {
	pending: i32, // damage shown locally but not yet confirmed by a delta
	basis:   i32, // authoritative hp at the last overlay update
	expires: f64, // overlay expiry time (seconds, caller's clock)
}
PHP_TTL :: 0.6 // seconds allowed for an authoritative hp update to arrive

php_note_hit :: proc "contextless" (ph: ^Predicted_Hp, hp_now: i32, amount: i32, now: f64)
php_display :: proc "contextless" (ph: ^Predicted_Hp, hp_now: i32, now: f64) -> i32

Call php_note_hit at visual contact and php_display when drawing health, as rock_impact in rocks.odin does. When the authoritative hp drop arrives, it consumes the overlay so the display does not subtract damage twice. If the host judges a miss, the overlay expires and the displayed bar returns to the authoritative value. php_display clamps to 1 while authoritative hp is positive, so speculative damage cannot display a death.

Publishing combat stats#

Call combat_columns once on the host to register the three stat columns. At impact, call credit_hit; on a killing blow, call credit_kill. The session then replicates and displays those recorded values.

Odin
Combat_Cols :: struct {
	damage: ksess.Stat_Col,
	kills:  ksess.Stat_Col,
	deaths: ksess.Stat_Col,
}
// Host, once at start: declare the standard combat columns (idempotent).
combat_columns :: proc(s: ^ksess.Session) -> Combat_Cols
// Host, at impact: record damage credit for a valid attacker.
credit_hit :: proc(s: ^ksess.Session, cols: Combat_Cols, attacker: knet.Player_Id, amount: i32)
// Host, on a killing blow.
credit_kill :: proc(s: ^ksess.Session, cols: Combat_Cols, attacker, victim: knet.Player_Id)

Pools#

pool_tick maintains a dynamic projectile array. It sweeps each tick's segment before stepping, removes a projectile on hit or expiry, and updates iteration correctly after removal. The game supplies target, hit, and expiry callbacks:

Odin
Slug :: struct { p: kcombat.Projectile, dmg: u8, shooter: knet.Player_Id }
flying: [dynamic]Slug                 // a wrapper pool (or a bare [dynamic]kcombat.Projectile)

kcombat.pool_tick(&self.flying, self, slug_targets, slug_hit, nil)   // hit-testing pool
kcombat.pool_tick(&self.lobs, self, nil, nil, lob_splash)            // fly-out-and-splash pool

targets runs separately for each projectile. If on_hit kills a target, the next projectile queries the updated target list. A hit always removes the projectile; the example pools do not support piercing. on_expire handles the end of its lifetime, such as applying a lob's splash damage.

Worked example#

From examples/cavecrawl/scripts/host.odin (cave_host_tick); the full pattern (launch on the command hook, announce the Fire, draw visuals per frame) is in rocks.odin:

Odin
kcombat.abilities_tick(sp.cds[:])   // per spelunker
kcombat.effects_tick(sp.fx[:])
// per flying rock:
from := fl.p.pos
alive := kcombat.projectile_step(&fl.p)
if hit, hit_ok := kcombat.projectile_hit(from, fl.p.vel, targets[:]); hit_ok {
	kcombat.credit_hit(&self.ses, self.cols, fl.shooter, ROCK_DMG)
	if kcombat.hit(&dw.hp, ROCK_DMG) { cave_slay_dweller(self, victim_id, fl.shooter) }
}

Timing and validation constraints#

  • Cooldowns and effect durations count network ticks. Convert a duration in seconds to ticks for the chosen rate. Only the authority decrements these values; clients receive the countdown through replication.
  • A cast near the end of a cooldown may be predicted differently on a client. The command is still sent, and the host decides acceptance.
  • Projectile.vel is per tick. Use the position before projectile_step for hit testing, and test that segment even if the step returns false: the last tick still occurred.
  • Carry the shooter's local cast origin and apply leash. The host's delayed position can otherwise launch the projectile along a different path.
